Testimony of Senator Pinny Beebe-Center Presenting
LD 1526, "An Act to Change the Permissible Hours and Penalties Pertaining to the Use of Consumer
Fireworks,"
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
May 5, 2025
Good afternoon Representative Hasenfus, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Pinny Beebe-Center, and I represent Senate District 12, which includes all of Knox County except for the Towns of Washington and Isle Au Haut. I am here today to present
LD 1526, "An Act to Change the Permissible Hours and Penalties Pertaining to the Use of Consumer
Fireworks."
I submitted this legislation on behalf of a constituent of mine, who had reached out because he was frustrated with the amount of fireworks that were constantly going off in my district over the summer. While I am one of countless people who enjoys a good fireworks show, I also understand that there is a time and place for these shows to happen, and there needs to be some guardrails put in place for not only our
neighbors peace of mind, but also for everyone's safety.
This bill changes the permissible hours in which fireworks can be set off to between 9 a.m. and 9 p.m.
However, on the Fourth ofJuly, New Year's Eve, and the weekends immediately before and after those holidays, fireworks may be set off between the hours of 9 a.m. and 12:30 a.m. These holidays are some that we typically associate with fireworks shows, so it makes sense to make the end time later. Having the end
time be at 9 p.m. normally will prevent these shows from going on long into the night, disturbing our neighbor's, in particular, their children and pets.
This bill also states that a person may use consumer fireworks only on their property or on the property of a person who has consented to having fireworks being used on their property. Violating either of these rules will result in a fine of no less than $100 and no more than $1,000.
While I love a good fireworks show, we need to also be considerate of our neighbors. Some people have pets who may be frightened by fireworks constantly going off. Some of our neighbors may suffer from PTSD, and fireworks may trigger a PTSD response due to the loud explosions. I believe that these stipulations will help some of our neighbors have some peace of mind, and prevent long fireworks shows from going into the
night, disturbing people's sleep.
I thank you all for your time and consideration. I will do my best to answer what question you may have.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association

In Opposition to
LD 1526 --An Act to Change the Permissible Hours and Penalties Pertaining to the Use of Consumer
Fireworks

May 5, 2025

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal

Justice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham`, nd I am submitting testimony in

opposition to LD 1526, at the direction of MMA'

Com1niflee (LPC). Our LPC is made

up of individuals from across Maine with municipal officials elected by their peers across Maine's 35

Senate districts representing communities with very different access to available enforcement resources

and local capacity.

The primary opposition to the bill is centered on the need to change municipal ordinances to align with the new operating time proposed by the bill which will create a fiscal note. Most noise ordinances are established with a 10:00 p.m. cut off and in tourism destinations, the weekend fireworks are oflen associated with weddings and back yard celebrations that use the twilight period in peak summer hours afforded by the 10:00 p.m. cut off to allow for displays and do not require the use of a commercial
operator. A 9:00 p.m. cut off time will make consumer fireworks less likely to be seen, and more likely to
shift the consumer market to louder noise impacts.

Additionally, many communities limit the period of use for fireworks between the hours of 5 p.1n. and 10 p.m. to make sure adequate fire stafi are available for any resulting public safety hazard that the permitted use may cause. In these communities, the hours are extended to 12:30 a.m. only on July 4 and
January 31. This bill would upend those ordinances as well. A list of approaches municipalities have taken
towards fireworks ordinances is available here:
https://www.maine.gov/dps/fino/inspections/i'ireworks/ordinances
Increasing the fines and penalties makes sense as they are unusually low and not much of a
deterrent. Current municipal ordinance violations for consumer fireworks range between $500 and not more than $2,500 for each offense.

In Maine, as in most states, commercial (display) and consumer fireworks are regulated in different ways. The biggest difference in the regulatory scheme is that display fireworks require the licensing of those conducting the display and transporting the fireworks in addition to a permitting process for putting on the display. Within that framework are numerous rules focused on containers, distance, and other requirements necessary to put on
a large show safely. Display fireworks are much larger and more dangerous than consumer fireworks. Though
still very dangerous, use and possession of consumer fireworks is granted to most individuals over the age of eighteen without any restrictions or requirements to be trained or licensed to use them.

LD 1526, An Act to Change the Permissible Hours and Penalties Pertaining to the Use of
Consumer Fireworks I

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Criminal
Justice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Shawn Esler, and it is a privilege to serve as the State Fire Marshal. I write neither for or against LD 1526.

In preparation for my testimony, we conducted research on recent fireworks violations. In 2024,
across the State there were no violations written by law enforcement on Title 8, Sec 223-A (8)(A) pertaining to discharging consumer fireworks after or before permissible hours. In 2024, across the State only one (1) civil violation written by law enforcement on Title 8, Sec 223-A (8)(B) pertaining to the discharge of consumer fireworks that likely occurred on a property without the consent of the owner.

While the Fire Marshal's Office regulates the sale and use of fireworks across the State, we
would have no ability to effectively enforce the changes outlined in LD 1526. This bill would
likely impact local law enforcement, State Police, and Sheriff` s Offices responding to noise complaints regarding fireworks in their respective communities. For the purpose of discussion, State Police responded to approximately 230 noise complaints of the nearly 67,000 calls for service in 2024. This represents 0.34% of their annual calls for service. Likely only a few of the 230 were fireworks related, significantly lowering that percentage.
